item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ub159-rBwpc

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入了解為何一家尚無臨床產品的 AI 製藥公司 Isomorphic Labs，其估值能高達 500 億美元，揭示資本市場對生醫 AI 的底層邏輯與期望。
  • 剖析傳統新藥研發長達 15 年、耗資 15 億美元且臨床失敗率高達 90% 的結構性困境，理解現代藥物探索為何陷入停滯。
  • 掌握 DeepMind 與 AlphaFold 核心團隊如何運用通用平台、數據尺度定律及跨領域協作，突破傳統動物實驗瓶頸並實現研發的「知識複利」。

摘要

傳統新藥研發的困境與天價估值的衝擊

作者指出，傳統新藥研發面臨著平均週期長達 15 年、成本高達 15 億美元，且進入人體臨床後仍有 90% 候選藥物失敗的嚴酷現實。然而，由 AlphaFold 創造者、諾貝爾化學獎得主 Demis Hassabis 創立的 Isomorphic Labs，在尚未有任何藥物進入臨床試驗的情況下，正尋求高達 500 億美元的估值融資，該金額遠超全球 AI 製藥市場目前的總規模。作者藉由該公司總裁 Max Jaderberg 的視角，帶領觀眾深入剖析 AI 驅動新藥開發的真實挑戰與革命性潛力。

從遊戲 AI 轉向生物領域與研發複利概念

曾主導 AlphaGo 與 AlphaStar 專案的 Max Jaderberg 發現，儘管數十年來科學論文與藥物形式大幅增加，新藥獲批數量卻長期停滯，根本原因在於人類製藥本質上是高度依賴經驗的試錯過程，且每個專案都是孤立的客製化研究。Isomorphic Labs 的核心突圍策略在於建立一套底層通用平台，將不同藥物開發所獲得的疾病生物學和分子工程經驗全面回饋給系統，進而創造出傳統研發無法實現的知識複利效應。

跨領域團隊架構與實驗級精度的電腦模擬

在組織運作上，團隊以約五位頂級 AI 工程師搭配一位生物或化學專家的比例協作，由專家引導方向以確保模型成果能切實轉化為真實藥物。作者強調，新藥研發最龐大的成本其實耗費在人體臨床試驗，臨床失敗多半源於無法預料的脫靶毒性或連鎖負面反應。因此，Isomorphic Labs 的關鍵目標是打造具備實驗級精度的模擬與世界模型，盡可能將分子設計與機制驗證移至電腦上完成，在進入人體試驗前精準預警風險。

克服動物實驗局限與自動化實驗的反饋願景

針對數據來源，團隊放棄存在大量偏差的歷史數據，轉而自主設計並生成高品質訓練資料，成功驗證了尺度定律（Scaling Laws）在生物領域的有效性。此外，針對傳統動物實驗預測人體臨床毒性僅約 30% 準確率的短板，團隊致力於結合 AI 預測模型、類器官與器官晶片來直接評估人體毒性反應。雖然該公司積極籌建自動化機器人實驗室以縮短實驗驗證週期，但長遠願景仍是最大限度地減少對物理世界的依賴，在數位空間中完成全面的藥物重塑。

================================================

Hello everyone, welcome to Best Partners , I’m Da Fei. I'm not sure if you have a concept of new drug R&D, but the industry average cycle is 15 years, with an average cost of $ 1.5 billion, and ultimately 90%of candidate drugs that enter human trials still fail. These figures would be considered brutal in any industry, yet the pharmaceutical sector has been carrying this burden for decades. Recently, a company that doesn't even have a single drug in human clinical trials is negotiating a $ 5 billion funding round, with a valuation that could reach $ 50 billion. This company is Isomorphic Labs, backed by Google's parent company, and founded by. the creator of AlphaFold and Nobel laureate in Chemistry, Demis Hassabis. What kind of concept is $ 50 billion? The global AI drug discovery market in 2025 is only about $ 2.3 billion. How can a company without a single product in clinical trials justify a valuation more than 20 times the entire market size? In today's video, we will follow the logic of Isomorphic Labs President Max Jaderberg to break down AI-driven drug development, see where the real difficulties lie, and what AI can and cannot solve. Let’s start with the. company’s origins. Isomorphic Labs was founded in 2021 by Hassabis, with daily operations handed over to President Max Jaderberg. Jaderberg’s background is quite interesting; he is a computer vision Ph.D. from Oxford, his team won a championship in 2014, and that same year he sold his vision company to Google’s DeepMind. Afterward, he was deeply involved in projects like AlphaGo and AlphaStar, and worked on early generative and language models. Why would someone building gaming AI switch to drug discovery? Jaderberg’s own explanation is that back in 2018 and.

2019, when they were focused on whether AI could beat video games, they proved that systematic methods could solve seemingly impossible problems step by step. After that, he began to wonder which truly important problems this mature technology of deep learning and reinforcement learning should be applied to. The early success of AlphaFold gave him confidence; it was the first time it was verified that deep learning models could be effective within a crucial biological space. In 2021, he co-founded Isomorphic Labs with Hassabis, and he went on to discuss a very anomalous phenomenon: over the past few decades, scientific papers have increased 10 to. 20 times, and drug modalities have expanded to include antibodies, small molecules, and peptides, yet the number of new drugs approved annually remains nearly a flat line, stagnant for years. Even more absurdly, the R&D cost for each new drug has risen from hundreds of millions to 1.5 billion dollars, and the cycle has stretched from 8-9 years to 15 years. Knowledge is exploding, yet drug development is becoming more expensive and difficult. What is the reason for this? What Hassabis feels most deeply is that the essence of human drug discovery has always been a process highly dependent on empirical trial and error. Thousands of years ago, it relied on luck; later, it evolved into organized. trial and error. For many classic drugs , we initially had no idea how they worked. Aspirin and Prozac were used for a long time, and we still didn't know how they functioned in the body. To this day, most of the industry still follows this process: propose a disease mechanism hypothesis, propose a molecular design hypothesis, synthesize the molecule, test it in the real world , and then iterate repeatedly. This process is extremely slow, and it is very difficult to obtain clear feedback signals. Another even bigger problem is that biology itself is too complex. Cells are high-temperature chaotic systems, and the number of possible molecular design combinations is too.

vast to exhaust. The only tools humans have are still based on trial-and-error screening, which determines that there is an upper limit to the complexity of solutions you can find within limited time and funding. The "low-hanging fruit " that could once be picked through empirical trial and error are being plucked one by one, and the complexity of the remaining "hard nuts to crack" is already beyond the reach of traditional methods. Additionally, traditional drug development treats every drug as an isolated, highly customized, and cutting-edge research project. You learn a massive amount of knowledge on a single project, but it is very difficult to transfer that to the next one. AI happens to be able to change this. If. you build a universal platform at the base layer and use it to develop drugs one after another, this platform can continuously absorb the experience from every real-world application, iterating on the fundamental understanding of disease biology and molecular engineering. The more drugs you develop this way, the stronger the platform becomes, truly creating compound interest in R&D. This is the core path of Isomorphic Labs. They are not the first to use AI for drug discovery, but using a universal base-layer platform to achieve knowledge compounding is their biggest shift compared to previous attempts. Now that we've discussed "why ," let's talk about "how." First, it’s about the people. AI drug discovery is a. cross-disciplinary field with a very short history; there are simply no ready-made AI drug discovery experts in the talent market. Isomorphic Labs ' strategy is straightforward: recruit the world's top talent in pure AI and deep learning, even if they have zero knowledge of life sciences or chemistry , as long as they want their work to make a real impact. At the same time, they hire the best experts in biology and chemistry—even those without prior AI experience—and through high-frequency communication and mutual learning, slowly cultivate true interdisciplinary scientists internally. What is the specific ratio? For core AI model projects, it's roughly five AI engineers.

to one domain expert. Where these few experts are truly effective is in helping the team maintain focus, ensuring that everyone doesn't chase false metrics that aren't grounded in reality, but instead creates something that can truly become a drug. In terms of their roadmap, Isomorphic Labs' North Star goal is to move drug discovery, molecular design, and the understanding of disease biology onto computers as much as possible. What they value most is having their simulation and world models reach experimental-grade precision. Take AlphaFold, for example: previously, resolving a protein structure required months or even years of X-ray crystallography experiments, but now models can predict it directly,. saving a massive amount of time. On every internal model leaderboard at Isomorphic Labs, there is a dashed line representing experimental precision, and the goal is for models to cross that line. Once it’s crossed, there’s no need for frequent lab work, as a vast amount of drug design can be completed on a computer. Why is this so important? Because the real cost of new drug development isn't in the initial in vitro or small-scale experiments, which only account for about two to three years and around 50 million dollars. The remaining 1.45 billion dollars and 12 years are actually consumed by long and arduous human clinical trials. The root. cause of clinical failure is that, before the drug is given to patients, humans simply cannot foresee those issues. It is only upon reaching clinical trials that unexpected toxic side effects are discovered, or that a molecule hits the intended target but also accidentally hits another, or even that the target itself is hit correctly , but modulating that target triggers other negative chain reactions in the human body. Therefore, the real opportunity lies in clearly identifying these risks before entering clinical trials. So, where does the data come from? This is a critical question. There are indeed many massive databases on the market, but many of them are just.

byproducts of years of daily drug manufacturing, and they may carry strong biases. If you want a model capable of generalization to solve the drug discovery puzzle, this biased historical data often doesn't help. Isomorphic Labs 'choice is to get hands-on, specifically designing and generating their own training data, and they have already clearly observed the scaling laws of data taking effect in the field of biology. Another point worth mentioning is animal testing. Currently, regulators require proof that a molecule is non-toxic in mice and other animals, but. in reality, a drug proven safe in mice often still exhibits toxicity in the human body. The reason is simple: mice are not humans. Research findings vary, but generally speaking, animal experiments only have about a 30% accuracy rate in predicting human clinical toxicity. Demis Hassabis says that if his AI team brought him a model with only 30%accuracy, he would likely tell them to "do better." Yet, this is the current industry standard for using animal experiments to predict human clinical toxicity. Therefore, there is a huge opportunity here to redesign the. endpoints for predicting human clinical toxicity—moving beyond the animal testing framework and combining in vitro metrics, AI predictive models, organoids , organ-on-a-chip, and synthetic human tissues to model human clinical toxicity directly. This brings us to a very popular trend. Isomorphic Labs recently announced the establishment of a lab in San Francisco, which outsiders speculate is an attempt to build a robotic, automated closed-loop system. AI models need rapid feedback to iterate; code can clearly be tested for correctness immediately, but biological experiments often take three weeks to produce.

results. Robotic labs can accelerate this feedback loop. What is Demis Hassabis's take on this? He acknowledges that automated labs are advancing quickly, and Isomorphic Labs itself has worked with such labs for a long time, but ultimately, he wants to minimize reliance on the physical world because no matter how fast robots are, they will eventually hit the limits of the laws of physics. For example, synthesizing a molecule takes time, and culturing cells requires waiting days for them to reach the proper state; robots are powerless against these physical constraints. So, while automated labs are certainly worth pursuing, the focus of R&D should be. shifted entirely toward computer simulations. When you enter a real lab, the goal should be to verify hypotheses , not to explore and trial-and-error. Regarding their business model, Isomorphic Labs develops its AI drug design engine internally, but it does not sell the models, does not offer licensing, and does not charge by the token; it uses the engine directly to create drugs. Implementation is split into two paths: one is an internal resource pipeline, funded and advanced independently, with Isomorphic retaining all rights, focusing on oncology, immunology, and inflammatory diseases. The other is partnering with pharmaceutical or biotech companies, such as Eli Lilly, Novartis, or Johnson. &Johnson, where the partner provides disease biology knowledge and R&D, while Isomorphic Labs is responsible for converting it into candidate molecules, earning revenue through upfront payments , milestone payments, and future sales royalties. At the core of this lies a record platform called Sodde. In February 2020, SomicLabs first publicly disclosed some capabilities of this AI drug design engine. Fold3 is already capable of predicting the interaction structures between proteins and other molecules. However, when faced with new targets or molecules lacking representative training data, prediction.

accuracy drops. Sodde attempts to improve the model's generalization ability on these unknown systems; on the RNprocess benchmark designed to test generalization, Sodde's structural prediction accuracy on complex systems with large training data disparities is more than double that of AlphaFold3. Regarding the prediction of antibody-antigen binding interfaces, Sodde’s performance in the high-precision range also outperforms AlphaFold3 and similar open-source models like RoseTTAFold2. Sodde can also predict the binding affinity between molecules and target proteins; without relying on experimentally resolved crystal structures, it completes. predictions much faster than traditional physical simulations, with accuracy approaching high-precision physical simulation methods. Let’s discuss another interesting angle: multi-drug combinations. Back then, controlling HIV didn't rely on a single drug, but on cocktail therapy; yet, many cancer treatments are still developed as monotherapies. Why aren't there more cocktail therapies for cancer? The root cause is that the molecules themselves aren't precise enough; many drugs are effective but carry toxicity or cause liver damage, and when patients take several such drugs, harmful interactions can occur. Ultimately, it is because. past precision in molecular engineering was insufficient, limiting the possibilities for combination therapy. AI can play a role here. If we can design molecules with extreme precision —safe enough to spare the liver and free from negative mutual interference—it becomes much more feasible to design complex multi-drug combinations, regulating an entire set of targets across complex biological pathways rather than just focusing on a single one. Lastly, let's talk about the timeline and prospects; SomicLabs expects to initiate its first human clinical trials by the end of 2026. Early clinical trials focus primarily on safety and tolerability; there is still.

a long way to go before proving these drugs are truly effective. Jed Buchwald uses a baseball game to describe the development stage, believing the team is currently in the first inning. If we fast-forward five years, he would be very disappointed if humanity hasn't achieved a qualitative leap in its predictive capabilities for biological systems, or if the ability to precisely design low-toxicity molecules hasn't significantly improved. Regarding longevity, he has his own judgment; conquering cancer and heart disease can indeed extend lifespan, but as people age, various chronic issues associated with aging will still continue to accumulate. Even if you live to be eighty or ninety, the last ten or twenty. years of life may see a significant drop in quality, with bone and muscle degeneration leading to limited mobility and a decline in mental health. So he focuses on two directions: first, extending healthy lifespan by treating various age-related diseases, and second , directly intervening in the aging roots that cause cellular, organ, and bodily decline. Returning to the initial question, why is a company with no drugs in clinical trials worth $ 50 billion? Beyond the market potential of Drug A, the SMOP Labs team is truly elite. Chief Scientist Miles Congreve has over 25 years of drug discovery experience and. is a co-inventor of the marketed breast cancer drug KISC. Chief Research Officer Celeste Strack is responsible for research strategy and the drug discovery pipeline. Chief Medical Officer Ben Urf is responsible for advancing drug candidates into clinical trials, and Chief Technology Officer Sergey Yakunin has over 20 years of experience in engineering and machine learning. The Scientific Advisory Board also includes CRISPR gene-editing pioneer and 2020 Nobel Laureate in Chemistry Jennifer Doudna, as well as 2021 Nobel Laureate in Chemistry David MacMillan. From early molecular design to clinical development , this support team covers multiple key.

stages of drug research and development . Although the large financing provides ample funds for later-stage R&D, whether this bet will ultimately pay off still depends on the clinical trial results to be released over the next few years. The path of drug development makes sense logically and has seen progress, but the real test has yet to begin. Thanks for watching, and see you in the next episode.

一家尚无药物进入临床试验的公司，估值却可能达到 500 亿美元，是 2025 年全球 AI 药物发现市场规模的 20 多倍。这家公司就是 Alphabet 旗下的 Isomorphic Labs。本期从其创始人背景、技术路径、人才策略、商业模式到核心技术平台 IsoDDE，系统拆解 AI 制药的底层逻辑：为什么新药研发越做越慢、动物实验为何只有 30% 预测准确率、自动化实验室能否突破物理边界、AI 能否让癌症也用上"鸡尾酒疗法"。预计 2026 年底启动首次人体临床试验，这场押注最终能否兑现，仍需等待临床数据说话。

To this day, most of the industry still follows this process: propose a disease mechanism hypothesis, propose a molecular design hypothesis, synthesize the molecule, test it in the real world , and then iterate repeatedly. This process is extremely slow, and it is very difficult to obtain clear feedback signals. Another even bigger problem is that biology itself is too complex. Cells are high-temperature chaotic systems, and the number of possible molecular design combinations is too.

vast to exhaust. The only tools humans have are still based on trial-and-error screening, which determines that there is an upper limit to the complexity of solutions you can find within limited time and funding. The "low-hanging fruit " that could once be picked through empirical trial and error are being plucked one by one, and the complexity of the remaining "hard nuts to crack" is already beyond the reach of traditional methods. Additionally, traditional drug development treats every drug as an isolated, highly customized, and cutting-edge research project. You learn a massive amount of knowledge on a single project, but it is very difficult to transfer that to the next one. AI happens to be able to change this. If. you build a universal platform at the base layer and use it to develop drugs one after another, this platform can continuously absorb the experience from every real-world application, iterating on the fundamental understanding of disease biology and molecular engineering. The more drugs you develop this way, the stronger the platform becomes, truly creating compound interest in R&D. This is the core path of Isomorphic Labs. They are not the first to use AI for drug discovery, but using a universal base-layer platform to achieve knowledge compounding is their biggest shift compared to previous attempts. Now that we've discussed "why ," let's talk about "how." First, it’s about the people. AI drug discovery is a. cross-disciplinary field with a very short history; there are simply no ready-made AI drug discovery experts in the talent market. Isomorphic Labs ' strategy is straightforward: recruit the world's top talent in pure AI and deep learning, even if they have zero knowledge of life sciences or chemistry , as long as they want their work to make a real impact. At the same time, they hire the best experts in biology and chemistry—even those without prior AI experience—and through high-frequency communication and mutual learning, slowly cultivate true interdisciplinary scientists internally. What is the specific ratio? For core AI model projects, it's roughly five AI engineers.

to one domain expert. Where these few experts are truly effective is in helping the team maintain focus, ensuring that everyone doesn't chase false metrics that aren't grounded in reality, but instead creates something that can truly become a drug. In terms of their roadmap, Isomorphic Labs' North Star goal is to move drug discovery, molecular design, and the understanding of disease biology onto computers as much as possible. What they value most is having their simulation and world models reach experimental-grade precision. Take AlphaFold, for example: previously, resolving a protein structure required months or even years of X-ray crystallography experiments, but now models can predict it directly,. saving a massive amount of time. On every internal model leaderboard at Isomorphic Labs, there is a dashed line representing experimental precision, and the goal is for models to cross that line. Once it’s crossed, there’s no need for frequent lab work, as a vast amount of drug design can be completed on a computer. Why is this so important? Because the real cost of new drug development isn't in the initial in vitro or small-scale experiments, which only account for about two to three years and around 50 million dollars. The remaining 1.45 billion dollars and 12 years are actually consumed by long and arduous human clinical trials. The root. cause of clinical failure is that, before the drug is given to patients, humans simply cannot foresee those issues. It is only upon reaching clinical trials that unexpected toxic side effects are discovered, or that a molecule hits the intended target but also accidentally hits another, or even that the target itself is hit correctly , but modulating that target triggers other negative chain reactions in the human body. Therefore, the real opportunity lies in clearly identifying these risks before entering clinical trials. So, where does the data come from? This is a critical question. There are indeed many massive databases on the market, but many of them are just.

byproducts of years of daily drug manufacturing, and they may carry strong biases. If you want a model capable of generalization to solve the drug discovery puzzle, this biased historical data often doesn't help. Isomorphic Labs 'choice is to get hands-on, specifically designing and generating their own training data, and they have already clearly observed the scaling laws of data taking effect in the field of biology. Another point worth mentioning is animal testing. Currently, regulators require proof that a molecule is non-toxic in mice and other animals, but. in reality, a drug proven safe in mice often still exhibits toxicity in the human body. The reason is simple: mice are not humans. Research findings vary, but generally speaking, animal experiments only have about a 30% accuracy rate in predicting human clinical toxicity. Demis Hassabis says that if his AI team brought him a model with only 30%accuracy, he would likely tell them to "do better." Yet, this is the current industry standard for using animal experiments to predict human clinical toxicity. Therefore, there is a huge opportunity here to redesign the. endpoints for predicting human clinical toxicity—moving beyond the animal testing framework and combining in vitro metrics, AI predictive models, organoids , organ-on-a-chip, and synthetic human tissues to model human clinical toxicity directly. This brings us to a very popular trend. Isomorphic Labs recently announced the establishment of a lab in San Francisco, which outsiders speculate is an attempt to build a robotic, automated closed-loop system. AI models need rapid feedback to iterate; code can clearly be tested for correctness immediately, but biological experiments often take three weeks to produce.

results. Robotic labs can accelerate this feedback loop. What is Demis Hassabis's take on this? He acknowledges that automated labs are advancing quickly, and Isomorphic Labs itself has worked with such labs for a long time, but ultimately, he wants to minimize reliance on the physical world because no matter how fast robots are, they will eventually hit the limits of the laws of physics. For example, synthesizing a molecule takes time, and culturing cells requires waiting days for them to reach the proper state; robots are powerless against these physical constraints. So, while automated labs are certainly worth pursuing, the focus of R&D should be. shifted entirely toward computer simulations. When you enter a real lab, the goal should be to verify hypotheses , not to explore and trial-and-error. Regarding their business model, Isomorphic Labs develops its AI drug design engine internally, but it does not sell the models, does not offer licensing, and does not charge by the token; it uses the engine directly to create drugs. Implementation is split into two paths: one is an internal resource pipeline, funded and advanced independently, with Isomorphic retaining all rights, focusing on oncology, immunology, and inflammatory diseases. The other is partnering with pharmaceutical or biotech companies, such as Eli Lilly, Novartis, or Johnson. &Johnson, where the partner provides disease biology knowledge and R&D, while Isomorphic Labs is responsible for converting it into candidate molecules, earning revenue through upfront payments , milestone payments, and future sales royalties. At the core of this lies a record platform called Sodde. In February 2020, SomicLabs first publicly disclosed some capabilities of this AI drug design engine. Fold3 is already capable of predicting the interaction structures between proteins and other molecules. However, when faced with new targets or molecules lacking representative training data, prediction.

accuracy drops. Sodde attempts to improve the model's generalization ability on these unknown systems; on the RNprocess benchmark designed to test generalization, Sodde's structural prediction accuracy on complex systems with large training data disparities is more than double that of AlphaFold3. Regarding the prediction of antibody-antigen binding interfaces, Sodde’s performance in the high-precision range also outperforms AlphaFold3 and similar open-source models like RoseTTAFold2. Sodde can also predict the binding affinity between molecules and target proteins; without relying on experimentally resolved crystal structures, it completes. predictions much faster than traditional physical simulations, with accuracy approaching high-precision physical simulation methods. Let’s discuss another interesting angle: multi-drug combinations. Back then, controlling HIV didn't rely on a single drug, but on cocktail therapy; yet, many cancer treatments are still developed as monotherapies. Why aren't there more cocktail therapies for cancer? The root cause is that the molecules themselves aren't precise enough; many drugs are effective but carry toxicity or cause liver damage, and when patients take several such drugs, harmful interactions can occur. Ultimately, it is because. past precision in molecular engineering was insufficient, limiting the possibilities for combination therapy. AI can play a role here. If we can design molecules with extreme precision —safe enough to spare the liver and free from negative mutual interference—it becomes much more feasible to design complex multi-drug combinations, regulating an entire set of targets across complex biological pathways rather than just focusing on a single one. Lastly, let's talk about the timeline and prospects; SomicLabs expects to initiate its first human clinical trials by the end of 2026. Early clinical trials focus primarily on safety and tolerability; there is still.

a long way to go before proving these drugs are truly effective. Jed Buchwald uses a baseball game to describe the development stage, believing the team is currently in the first inning. If we fast-forward five years, he would be very disappointed if humanity hasn't achieved a qualitative leap in its predictive capabilities for biological systems, or if the ability to precisely design low-toxicity molecules hasn't significantly improved. Regarding longevity, he has his own judgment; conquering cancer and heart disease can indeed extend lifespan, but as people age, various chronic issues associated with aging will still continue to accumulate. Even if you live to be eighty or ninety, the last ten or twenty. years of life may see a significant drop in quality, with bone and muscle degeneration leading to limited mobility and a decline in mental health. So he focuses on two directions: first, extending healthy lifespan by treating various age-related diseases, and second , directly intervening in the aging roots that cause cellular, organ, and bodily decline. Returning to the initial question, why is a company with no drugs in clinical trials worth $ 50 billion? Beyond the market potential of Drug A, the SMOP Labs team is truly elite. Chief Scientist Miles Congreve has over 25 years of drug discovery experience and. is a co-inventor of the marketed breast cancer drug KISC. Chief Research Officer Celeste Strack is responsible for research strategy and the drug discovery pipeline. Chief Medical Officer Ben Urf is responsible for advancing drug candidates into clinical trials, and Chief Technology Officer Sergey Yakunin has over 20 years of experience in engineering and machine learning. The Scientific Advisory Board also includes CRISPR gene-editing pioneer and 2020 Nobel Laureate in Chemistry Jennifer Doudna, as well as 2021 Nobel Laureate in Chemistry David MacMillan. From early molecular design to clinical development , this support team covers multiple key.

stages of drug research and development . Although the large financing provides ample funds for later-stage R&D, whether this bet will ultimately pay off still depends on the clinical trial results to be released over the next few years. The path of drug development makes sense logically and has seen progress, but the real test has yet to begin. Thanks for watching, and see you in the next episode.

一家尚无药物进入临床试验的公司，估值却可能达到 500 亿美元，是 2025 年全球 AI 药物发现市场规模的 20 多倍。这家公司就是 Alphabet 旗下的 Isomorphic Labs。本期从其创始人背景、技术路径、人才策略、商业模式到核心技术平台 IsoDDE，系统拆解 AI 制药的底层逻辑：为什么新药研发越做越慢、动物实验为何只有 30% 预测准确率、自动化实验室能否突破物理边界、AI 能否让癌症也用上"鸡尾酒疗法"。预计 2026 年底启动首次人体临床试验，这场押注最终能否兑现，仍需等待临床数据说话。

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ub159-rBwpc

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入了解為何一家尚無臨床產品的 AI 製藥公司 Isomorphic Labs，其估值能高達 500 億美元，揭示資本市場對生醫 AI 的底層邏輯與期望。
  • 剖析傳統新藥研發長達 15 年、耗資 15 億美元且臨床失敗率高達 90% 的結構性困境，理解現代藥物探索為何陷入停滯。
  • 掌握 DeepMind 與 AlphaFold 核心團隊如何運用通用平台、數據尺度定律及跨領域協作，突破傳統動物實驗瓶頸並實現研發的「知識複利」。

摘要

傳統新藥研發的困境與天價估值的衝擊

作者指出，傳統新藥研發面臨著平均週期長達 15 年、成本高達 15 億美元，且進入人體臨床後仍有 90% 候選藥物失敗的嚴酷現實。然而，由 AlphaFold 創造者、諾貝爾化學獎得主 Demis Hassabis 創立的 Isomorphic Labs，在尚未有任何藥物進入臨床試驗的情況下，正尋求高達 500 億美元的估值融資，該金額遠超全球 AI 製藥市場目前的總規模。作者藉由該公司總裁 Max Jaderberg 的視角，帶領觀眾深入剖析 AI 驅動新藥開發的真實挑戰與革命性潛力。

從遊戲 AI 轉向生物領域與研發複利概念

曾主導 AlphaGo 與 AlphaStar 專案的 Max Jaderberg 發現，儘管數十年來科學論文與藥物形式大幅增加，新藥獲批數量卻長期停滯，根本原因在於人類製藥本質上是高度依賴經驗的試錯過程，且每個專案都是孤立的客製化研究。Isomorphic Labs 的核心突圍策略在於建立一套底層通用平台，將不同藥物開發所獲得的疾病生物學和分子工程經驗全面回饋給系統，進而創造出傳統研發無法實現的知識複利效應。

跨領域團隊架構與實驗級精度的電腦模擬

在組織運作上，團隊以約五位頂級 AI 工程師搭配一位生物或化學專家的比例協作，由專家引導方向以確保模型成果能切實轉化為真實藥物。作者強調，新藥研發最龐大的成本其實耗費在人體臨床試驗，臨床失敗多半源於無法預料的脫靶毒性或連鎖負面反應。因此，Isomorphic Labs 的關鍵目標是打造具備實驗級精度的模擬與世界模型，盡可能將分子設計與機制驗證移至電腦上完成，在進入人體試驗前精準預警風險。

克服動物實驗局限與自動化實驗的反饋願景

針對數據來源，團隊放棄存在大量偏差的歷史數據，轉而自主設計並生成高品質訓練資料，成功驗證了尺度定律（Scaling Laws）在生物領域的有效性。此外，針對傳統動物實驗預測人體臨床毒性僅約 30% 準確率的短板，團隊致力於結合 AI 預測模型、類器官與器官晶片來直接評估人體毒性反應。雖然該公司積極籌建自動化機器人實驗室以縮短實驗驗證週期，但長遠願景仍是最大限度地減少對物理世界的依賴，在數位空間中完成全面的藥物重塑。

一家尚无药物进入临床试验的公司，估值却可能达到 500 亿美元，是 2025 年全球 AI 药物发现市场规模的 20 多倍。这家公司就是 Alphabet 旗下的 Isomorphic Labs。本期从其创始人背景、技术路径、人才策略、商业模式到核心技术平台 IsoDDE，系统拆解 AI 制药的底层逻辑：为什么新药研发越做越慢、动物实验为何只有 30% 预测准确率、自动化实验室能否突破物理边界、AI 能否让癌症也用上"鸡尾酒疗法"。预计 2026 年底启动首次人体临床试验，这场押注最终能否兑现，仍需等待临床数据说话。

item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PWeHBBBh_10

值得閱讀的理由

  • 從 NVIDIA 創辦人黃仁勳可能離任的假設出發，說明領導人變動如何牽動公司治理、產業供應鏈與全球 AI 發展。
  • 比較對中國晶片與 AI 的不同管制思路，呈現遠端運算、晶片出口及開源合作之間的利害關係。
  • 深入分析 NVIDIA 對黃仁勳個人決策與信用的依賴，以及接班問題可能帶來的風險。
  • 整理 NVIDIA 長期押注新技術、分配算力資源和支持雲端業者的策略，理解公司成功背後的代價。

摘要

黃仁勳離任可能牽動的不只是 NVIDIA

作者 Da Fei 引述 Sanalysis 的文章，探討假如黃仁勳離開 NVIDIA，公司與產業可能如何改變。文章所談的不只是接班，更包括晶片如何分配、雲端業者如何取得融資與算力，以及全球 AI 發展能否維持速度。作者也提到一種尚未證實的猜測：黃仁勳離任可能與大量 GPU 流向中國的爭議有關。相關追蹤資料據稱顯示，仍有超過 1.5 吉瓦的受限制 NVIDIA 晶片進入中國，但這只是推測所依據的材料，並非定論。

晶片管制與美中 AI 生態

作者指出，美國國會已通過《遠端存取安全法》（RASA），後續仍待參議院處理；若黃仁勳這位反對設計不良限制措施的重要聲音離開，對中國 AI 與晶片的限制可能加速。作者認為，全面禁止並非唯一選項：讓中國研究團隊透過可信任的海外雲端遠端使用 GPU，能使收益留在美國企業手中，也讓美方掌握使用情況，必要時還可迅速中止存取。相較之下，禁止實體出口、同時限制可信雲端服務的做法，可能反而損害美國利益。

美國晶片業仍仰賴中國供應鏈與工程人才，AI 生態也會使用中國企業、學生及獨立研究者公開的成果。若中國仍能使用 NVIDIA 晶片，轉向本土加速器的誘因也可能較弱。因此，作者主張可以管制流向中國研究機構的總算力，但應考慮《MATCH 法案》式的做法，而非採取一刀切的 RASA 模式。此外，開源社群正協助中國研究團隊最佳化核心程式與模型；若政策使這類合作萎縮，美國新創與開源生態也可能失去重要的公開成果與模型基礎。

高度集中的領導模式與接班難題

作者認為，NVIDIA 長期以黃仁勳為核心運作，組織結構因此與一般大型企業不同。黃仁勳曾表示自己約有 60 名直屬部屬，並認為執行長應直接管理更多人；公司職稱與匯報關係未必代表職務重要性。這種精簡、扁平的運作方式，有助減少內耗，讓公司迅速調整方向，但也讓許多重大決策集中在他一人手中。產品與工程設計常被推進到極晚才定案，以保留調整空間；這種近似新創公司的速度，伴隨的是領導梯隊不夠深厚的風險。

作者指出，NVIDIA 公開曝光的高階主管不多，許多直接向黃仁勳匯報的主管缺乏對外歷練，也不一定有機會建立獨立領導聲望。文中提及的潛在人選包括負責超大規模資料中心與高效能運算業務的 Ian Buck，以及主管 GPU 工程的 Jonah Alben；兩人都具備豐富經驗，但仍難以完全接手黃仁勳對整個硬體、供應鏈與業務的掌控。財務長柯蕾特・克雷斯（Colette Kress）雖暫代相關職務，作者認為長期接班人未必會出自財務部門。更棘手的是，接任者不僅要有能力，還得整合數十位副總裁並維持共同願景，而高階主管未必願意承擔這項工作。

長期押注與黃仁勳的個人信用

作者認為 NVIDIA 最重要的優勢之一，是敢於押注需要多年甚至十年才能回收的技術。黃仁勳曾在內部反對聲中，將資源投入可程式化著色器與 Tensor Core；如今，機器人、自駕車、Omniverse 和 DGX Cloud 等領域，也被視為需要長期投入的布局。這些業務未必立刻帶來可觀獲利，但創辦人與董事會支持下的決策方式，讓公司能承受多年等待。若換成必須頻繁向董事會與股東交代的非創辦人執行長，這類高風險、長週期的投資可能更難延續。

黃仁勳的角色也不只在技術與產品決策上。他會決定晶片如何分配給大型雲端業者、新興雲端服務商，以及由 NVIDIA 信用支持、並分享雲端營收的計畫。作者形容，NVIDIA 有如「中央銀行」般居於算力與資金安排的核心，而市場對這種安排的信任，部分來自黃仁勳個人的信用與承諾。客戶購買的因而不只是 GPU，也包括他所代表的合作保證；下一任執行長能否建立同等信任，仍是未知數。

影片末段提出的財務問題

影片最後轉向 NVIDIA 財務與表外項目的議題，提到 2026 年 7 月 26 日、NVIDIA 2027 財年第二季，以及將六類表外項目加總分析的做法。不過字幕在作者開始說明計算方式時便中斷，因此這部分的分析與結論並未完整呈現。

================================================

Hello everyone, this is Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. If Jensen Huang leaves NVIDIA, is it only the company's head that is affected? Probably not; how chips are allocated, what cloud providers use for financing, who gets priority for storage capacity, and even whether global AI models can continue to evolve rapidly, could all change as a result. Because for the past 33 years, NVIDIA hasn't just been managed by Jensen Huang; it has largely been designed around him. After Jensen Huang announced his departure, Sanalysis published an article attempting to answer the question: what would NVIDIA. look like without him? Setting aside the rumors, what the article really aims to dissect is another layer of judgment— that the reason for his resignation may not be just a matter of conduct. One speculation being discussed repeatedly is that it is directly related to the massive flow of GPUs. Note that this is just speculation, not a conclusion. Supporting this speculation is a set of tracking data showing that over 1.5 gigawatts of restricted NVIDIA chips still entered China, and this doesn't even include the models specifically adjusted to bypass the rules. Under this system, the U.S. intelligence community. is believed to have played a major role in pushing for Jensen Huang's departure . What is more likely to happen is that the Remote Access Security Act, or similar legislation, will continue to move forward. It has already passed in the House of Representatives; next, it’s the Senate's turn. What is more worrying is that restrictions on AI and chips for China will likely accelerate significantly after losing their most staunch defender. Supporting some restrictions while believing they are poorly designed are not mutually exclusive; poorly designed restrictions can actually harm America's own interests. So, what exactly are the benefits of the current arrangement? Chinese labs can use GPUs remotely from. abroad instead of shipping the equipment into China. Profits stay with U.S. companies, the U.S. can monitor what these labs are doing, and when necessary , it can use political means or— coercive measures to cut off access almost instantly. Companies like NVIDIA , AMD, and Intel still rely on Chinese vendors for their supply chains, and NVIDIA and AMD still employ Chinese engineers in China for hardware and underlying software development. Without these people, the user experience would significantly deteriorate. The U.S. AI ecosystem also makes extensive use of publicly available research results from Chinese enterprises, students, and. independent researchers. Lastly, as long as China can still use NVIDIA, its incentive to shift toward domestic accelerators will be weaker. Therefore, the argument is not for total deregulation; restrictions can exist, but they should take the form of the MATCH Act rather than a one-size-fits-all approach like RASA. To be more specific, it means limiting the total computing power flowing to Chinese labs. While physical chip exports can be banned, remote access for trusted cloud providers should be maintained, following the same proliferation rules used during the Dennard scaling era. Another underestimated variable is open source, as it has been working directly with Chinese labs to help them optimize. kernels and models, and these labs are using Blackware. This is practically an open secret within the industry. If Jensen Huang leaves and the China hawks prevail, this cooperation will likely shrink, yet the U.S. open-source ecosystem and many startups are actually built upon these Chinese models and public achievements. However, for shareholders and the supply chain, the question is even more direct: what would NVIDIA look like without Jensen Huang? This company was never designed to operate without him. Jensen Huang has been at the helm for 33 years. Even if the board pushed him out, with the.

official narrative being a voluntary resignation, NVIDIA would still be significantly better off with him there . SpaceX and Tesla would not be the same without Musk; NVIDIA would be no different without Jensen Huang. NVIDIA’s organizational structure is quite anomalous for a company of its size. By his own account, he has about 60 direct reports. Jensen's reasoning is that a CEO should have the most direct reports because these people require the least management. He doesn’t even hold one-on-one meetings with these people, but the problem is that very few of them can accomplish things independently without him. The company is more like a. kingdom; there is only one king, and everyone else, regardless of their seniority, is simply executing his will . He has said that who reports to whom doesn't matter, and titles have nothing to do with the importance of a job. This is one reason NVIDIA can support such a high market cap with only about 42,000 employees. Fewer people means less internal friction and less office politics. This flat network gives employees more initiative and allows the company to keep up with the pace of technological change. So where does the speed come from? Once a direction is set , everyone pivots together. Product development and engineering are often pushed to the very last minute to keep. room for changing their minds. A former NVIDIA executive once noted that the design finalization for the GB200 was closer to the end of the product cycle than anyone would have liked. Jensen Huang himself has said he wants the company to remain in a startup state forever, but that, too, comes at a price . NVIDIA does not have a sufficiently deep bench of leadership. Just look at the official website: besides him, there are only five featured executives, two of whom are in Legal and Finance. Most direct reports have had no public-facing training, and are even explicitly discouraged from seeking exposure. Very few people go on to become CEOs at other tech giants after leaving the company,. though Arm’s Rene Haas is an exception. The reason is easy to understand: major decisions are concentrated in one person , leaving others little chance to prove themselves elsewhere. Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CFO, but a long-term successor is unlikely to come from a financial background. The most discussed internal candidates are Ian Buck and Jonah Alben. Buck developed the early prototypes at Stanford, joined Nvidia in 2004, and now leads the data center business as VP of Hyperscale and HPC. When Huang is traveling, he often oversees operations and frequently. speaks at meetings. Alben joined the company in 1997 and serves as Senior VP of GPU Engineering, overseeing GPU design. But realistically, no one can manage everything alone; they lack the ability to oversee all hardware engineering. While Alben has technical autonomy within his team, he does not control the entire chip stack. There are other senior leaders reporting to Jensen Huang who manage key technical and business units; both are excellent, but it is difficult for them to match Huang’s control over the supply chain. The successor issue is even trickier. A senior executive put it bluntly earlier. this year: "I'd rather die than take over Jensen Huang's job," simply because they don't want it. Alben is well-respected and capable, but similarly, no one truly wants the role. The situation has changed now that Kress has stepped in as interim, but aligning over 60 vice presidents under a unified company vision requires a very specific type of person, otherwise the company's direction will be lost in the noise. At its core, Nvidia's greatest strength is the courage to make bets that take many years, or even a decade, to pay off. Huang is one of the last old-school tech founders, from the same era as Elon Musk.

and slightly before Mark Zuckerberg. The companies that grew alongside his have largely been handed over to professional managers, including AMD, Google, Microsoft, Apple, and Amazon; only Nvidia still retains a founder-led decision-making style. With the support of the founder and the board, the company can take risks without fearing internal revolt, even after losing money for years. Wall Street analysts kept questioning, but Huang never wavered, and this final bet yielded a massive return. A former employee once noted that back then, use cases were very limited, and many internally opposed spending transistor budget on this. Yet. , he still bet the entire company on programmable shaders and tensor cores. Robotics and autonomous driving are the new bets, internally dubbed the " zero-dollar gamble." They make almost no money today, but Jensen Huang believes they will be as big as CUDA. The same logic applies to OMNIVERSE and DGX Cloud , as he needs to understand customers to design better products, even if these two businesses don't generate much profit and are eventually sidelined. However, if these decisions were made by a non-founder CEO, the accountability would be entirely different. Regardless of how long they stay at the company,. they face the board and shareholders, so such long-term bets and perseverance would significantly diminish. What is even harder to replicate is Jensen's role as a kingmaker and deal broker. How chips are allocated to cloud providers and who gets more has always been his call, with customers forever competing for his collaboration and attention. Moreover, an increasing number of deals require deep support from NVIDIA. Should more capacity go to hyperscalers, new cloud service providers, or those " bottom-line" projects backed by NVIDIA's credit that share in cloud revenue? The choice rests in his hands. This role of. NVIDIA as a central bank relies on the market's trust in him personally and his own credit. The next CEO will likely find it difficult to make such bold bets . Customers have never just bought GPUs ; they are also buying Jensen Huang's promise. Let’s first look at the date July 26, 2026, which is NVIDIA’s second quarter of fiscal year 2027. If we aggregate the six categories of off-balance-sheet items, the total commitments and guarantees amount to approximately $ 530 billion, compared to $ 184 billion the previous quarter. This includes $ 36 billion in capacity for new cloud providers, which is not easily. offloaded. The company also holds an equity investment portfolio worth $ 99 billion. The reason many customers want these deals isn't in the numbers. Global cloud providers are able to raise funds because Jensen Huang backs them, not because they chose NVIDIA after comparing all the options. NVIDIA’s backing allows these companies to secure financing even while bypassing the hyperscalers. They sell GPUs at full price on day one, then guarantee the buyer’s revenue, act as a guarantor for landlords, or sign the leases themselves , allowing operators without investment-grade ratings to borrow at investment-grade rates. Once this " Jensen Huang put option" ceases to exist , the entire ecosystem could face a significant contraction. The supply chain lockdown is highly personalized; if competitors could secure the same supply, their shipment volumes would be much higher. They can't because Jensen Huang personally went to Korea for storage and to Taiwan for chips. Nvidia has already locked in the supply of most logic, memory, and other critical components. He went to Korea in 2025 with the goal of securing memory before other executives realized just how severe the shortages would become. Many industry clients thought the 2026.

forecast was too aggressive, but later realized it was accurate. Nvidia's supply and capacity commitments jumped from $ 119 billion to $ 279 billion in a single quarter, with the main increase being memory. This type of lockdown carries a strong personal touch, as these deals were negotiated by him personally. An estimate suggests that SK Hynix's 2027 HBM4 price for Nvidia is about $ 3.0 to $ 3.3 per gigabit, while for other tier-one clients like AMD, Broadcom, and Google, it is $ 3.7 to $ 4.1. In exchange, it is believed within. the industry that there is a tacit understanding that Nvidia will give the SK Group priority GPU quotas. Without him, these companies would not prioritize Nvidia to the same extent, making it much easier for others to secure capacity. By 2028, over 70%of relevant capacity may shift toward non-Nvidia clients, a fact that is rarely mentioned. The reason the Taiwan supply chain is more willing to believe in this build-out and invest more boldly than anyone else is because of Jensen Huang’s vision. Those frequently mentioned supply chain dinners and commitments are the reason suppliers are willing to execute plans that are. extremely aggressive in terms of technology and logistics. At the same time, the entire AI industry would lose its chief spokesperson. Jensen Huang is everywhere—he is the most active advocate for AI and its face, a position no one can replace. He set Nvidia's China policy and led the push for open-source models. Open-source gives more countries, enterprises, and new cloud providers a reason to buy GPUs, rather than just the few frontier labs that are self-developing their own chips . When it comes to open-source, Nvidia needs it more than anyone else. Following current trends, it might only. have two real customers left: Epic and OpenAI. There are seven hyperscale cloud providers, and among these seven, all but SpaceX are attempting to develop their own specialized acceleration chips (XPUs) to cut into Nvidia's profits. Models and applications are complements to GPUs; this fact dictates that Nvidia must prioritize open-source. Frontier labs are also using Blackwell, and because Nvidia works closely with them, it has learned a great deal from these labs 'terminal usage. This feedback is transformed into innovations that expand the ecosystem, such as Mixture-of-Experts, DeepSeek, and. Deep-learning advancements, which are then disseminated to Western open-source communities and startups. With Nvidia’s potential departure, it is precisely these startups that will be hit the hardest. If they no longer have them as an advocate, continuing to provide funding and engineering support for open models, the situation will certainly change. Labs might stop open-sourcing kernel libraries that are clearly optimized for Blackwell, such as NIMX's MSA, DeepJAM, Deep-stack, or advanced FlashKDA, while global inference engines like SGL and VLLM all rely on these. innovations. At that point, they might have to deny using Nvidia GPUs, keeping all Nvidia-related software internal rather than open-source. This is not good news for the entire Nvidia ecosystem or the broader machine learning landscape. While this is certainly good for closed labs, it is detrimental to startups; furthermore, a company led by brokers is likely to sideline projects that are not performing well. Leading American models are becoming closed, and Nvidia is essentially single-handedly propping up the remainder of American open-source models. Their approach involves investing in companies like Reflection and Thinking-Posid, as well as acquiring.

Hugging Face. Nvidia has always been the party pushing for continued engagement with China, arguing that China should use and remain dependent on U.S. technology. With the H20 initially banned from entering China, only to be followed by hints of export licenses for Nvidia, this balancing act has long been difficult to maintain. It requires keeping China on the U.S. AI track while slowing down their self-development, all while restricting the quality and quantity of chips entering China. The question now is whether they were in a compromised position while pushing this agenda; this requires investigation to answer, but one thing is clear: the China hawks are winning the game. This. leads to a somewhat strange question: why now? This matter has been dug into for two consecutive rounds, and in the second round of investigations, there were five points where the intelligence foundation pointed directly to the U.S. intelligence community. The intelligence community has a significant stake in this matter. Trump, Rubio, and Lutnick were already aware of these conditions before the May visit; there are also claims that Lutnick had previously delayed chip strikes against China, but this relationship later changed, and the wind shifted in the other direction. As for Huang Le, the most likely scenario is that he is not a spy in the traditional sense, but rather a well-connected businessman. In China, it. is not unusual for well-connected business people to have contact with officials. To equate this directly with espionage is an oversimplification of the issue. On the other hand, the Department of Commerce now believes there are over 1.5 gigawatts of Nvidia chips in China that shouldn't be there. The winds of the midterm elections are blowing in favor of the Democrats. So, some people have decided to take action . They aim to both close loopholes in existing export controls and expand restrictions to completely cut off China's access to cutting-edge chips. The government is not unified on this issue. Trump used to provide cover for Lutnick, but no longer does; meanwhile,. the RASA passed by the House is awaiting a vote in the Senate. The process is as follows: RASA passed the House Foreign Affairs Committee 51-0 in April 2025, and passed the House 369-22 on January 12, 2026. Because it followed the suspension of rules procedure, which requires a two-thirds majority, the vote count shows it is quite popular. The bill was then sent to the Senate Banking Committee, where it has yet to be voted on; Nvidia and others have been lobbying hard against it. RASA is certainly not the only tool, but it is the one being most hotly discussed in Washington right. now. The problem is that its impact is global. It is understood that emerging cloud providers in Asia, Australia, Northern Europe, Europe, Canada, and even the U.S. are selling computing power to Chinese companies. Once this bill is enacted, they will all be affected; this is a global export control act with significant spillover effects. Jensen Huang doesn't want it to happen, and Lutnick likely doesn't either. So, we might want to think in reverse: even if recent headlines point in the same direction, passing RASA or similar bills could lead to unintended consequences. According to an old saying. in American politics, if politicians agree on something, it is highly likely to be a bad idea. The previously mentioned benefits still hold in this situation; more importantly, if Chinese labs are completely cut off from Nvidia GPUs, their incentive to turn to domestic accelerators will only grow stronger. And this is already happening . In February 2026, Zhipu announced GLM -5 support for seven types of domestic accelerators; in April 2026, DeepSeek published its V4 paper and open-sourced large kernels for Huawei Ascend NPUs used in V4P model inference. In June.

2026, Meituan released LCAT 2.0, with its pre-training entirely using Huawei Ascend 910B; politicians continue to underestimate how deeply intertwined China, Taiwan, and the U.S. really are. Many Chinese researchers work in top US labs, and many Chinese engineers at NVIDIA and AMD write the underlying code to get new chips running. Many Americans learn from Chinese open-source contributions, and many raw materials needed to make these chips also come from China, with many Tier 1 to Tier 6 ODMs and component suppliers being Chinese firms. Escalating tensions will. only lead to one result: fewer chips being made, and everyone's AI progress will slow down. This is why a better approach is to limit total computing power, rather than cutting off all contact. Banning exports while allowing trusted cloud providers to offer remote access is currently the best practice; as for the claim that servers are too heavy to fit in a backpack, a few ads can refute that. There are ads on Chinese social media, one for a cluster of 800 RTX 5090s, and another for a minimum of 1024. Jensen Huang said at Computex in May 2025 that the GB200 Blackwell system weighs nearly two tons. and couldn't possibly be stuffed into a pocket or backpack. But the problem was never how to move the whole machine, but rather how purchase orders and end-user documentation were falsified. On March 17, 2026, Supermicro's co-founder and head of sales, Leo Liang, as well as Taiwan sales head Steve Zhang and local contractor Willie Sun, were indicted. The indictment states that $ 2.5 billion in servers were sold to a Southeast Asian company, of which $ 510 million was smuggled into China. To pass the company's August 2025 audit and the Commerce Department's December 2025 audit, they set up decoy servers. The. indictment even includes a photo of Willie Sun and a friend using a hairdryer to peel off labels and serial number stickers from real servers to apply them to fake ones. The current status is that Leo has pleaded not guilty, and the trial date has been pushed from November 2, 2026, to March 29, 2027, because Supermicro was subpoenaed by the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, as disclosed in the company's 10-K filing on August 31. Willie faces four charges , including using decoy servers, impersonating a legal assistant named Mel, lying to officials during the December 2025 Commerce Department audit. , and deleting encrypted chat records on his phone the day he was arrested. He pleaded guilty on October 8, with sentencing set for September 8, 2027, while Steve Zhang is currently considered a fugitive. In the second case, nine people were indicted in Keelung involving 130 B300 units, 74 of which had already arrived in China earlier this year. The list includes a senior manager from NVIDIA's Taiwan office, who is identified as a key figure, along with two sales managers from Supermicro Taiwan, a CEO of a Supermicro distributor, a president of a server reseller, a project manager at a data center operator, and the head of a. freight forwarding company. The matter was discovered by accident. In May 2026 , while investigating a drug smuggling case, the Taiwan Coast Guard stumbled upon this batch of servers, detained three people, and subsequently searched multiple locations, seizing 56 servers, luxury cars, and approximately 9 million New Taiwan dollars in cash, equivalent to about 275,000 U.S. dollars. Starting in June, personnel from Supermicro and related companies were indicted one after another. In July, the senior manager from NVIDIA was charged, and by August, all nine defendants had been indicted. The first court hearing for this senior manager is set for October 16. The methods were actually not.

complicated: using shell companies, falsifying audits, forging documents, including creating a fake Supermicro website to display export licenses, and then declaring Japan as the export destination before transshipping to China. According to current procedures, any order exceeding eight units triggers an on-site inspection by Supermicro. In September 2025, that reseller obtained a purchase permit for 130 units, listing themselves as the end-user and even passing an on-site inspection at a data center, but prosecutors say the site did not meet rack space or power requirements and lacked even a signed lease agreement. Both cases are still. under trial; an indictment is not a conviction. As for why now, the most likely explanation is to clear the path for an extremely hawkish export control bill against China. Congress has just undergone a major shift in power, and with the end-of-year session approaching , removing the opposition first makes the bill easier to pass. This is one interpretation of Washington's actions, but it remains merely speculation. So, returning to the initial question, what would NVIDIA become without Jensen Huang ? At this scale and magnitude, the only case of a company performing well after the departure of a visionary founder is almost exclusively Apple after Steve. Jobs. Huang’s departure would likely mark the end of the era of visionary founders. To use an analogy, no one wants to drive a car built by someone else at 150 miles per hour, yet Jensen Huang drove it that way with ease. Whoever is pushed forward to maintain the status quo and lead the company from a founder-led model to a manager-led one will have to face a happy problem: what to do with all that cash? Huang’s line of thinking is clear: use the balance sheet to back the entire ecosystem, expanding credit for new cloud service providers and labs; this is a natural extension of supply chain advantages. Professional managers will likely do. another thing that makes equal sense: stock buybacks. Apple after Steve Jobs is the most successful example on this scale. The same script could very well play out all over again. The founder exits, the company turns conservative, and cash is returned to shareholders; shareholders may be satisfied, but the company won't push technology forward like it once did. This is not a good outcome for technology, and I fear it’s not for shareholders either. Jensen Huang will be missed, because Nvidia, a once-unique company, is becoming more ordinary. Internal friction and digestion will manifest both within the firm and across the global supply chain , which will shift from following one. man's bold vision to a manager's mediocre one. Without him, the tech world would look entirely different. As for succession, the current assessment is that Colette Kress is the most likely frontrunner, with Ajay Puri close behind . Among the potential external candidates, John Slattery has been mentioned. Given Nvidia's unique nature , internal promotion is more appropriate , yet the pool is already small, and it's still unclear if anyone is even willing to take the helm. Only top-tier industry figures could stand alongside Jensen Huang, and there is skepticism about whether CEOs like Lisa Su or Hock Tan could truly step into the role. Kress and Slattery are considered the best alternatives; regardless of who it is, one thing is certain: this is good news for Nvidia's competitors and bad news for its supply chain. Thanks for watching, and see you next time.

=============
